PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE
In 1963 the Psi Upsilon Fraternity, after much
study, instituted a
Program which emphasized the
modernization of our
operations. Among other things,
the new
program provided for a
larger and more com
municative "Diamond," a full time knowledgeable
operating staff at headquarters and Chapter Standards
to serve as a
guide to our
chapters. The Convention
called for the study of our Constitution with a
promise
to amend it so that it would be more in step with
today's educational world.
We spent most of last year acquainting our under
graduates and Alumni with the significance of the
Program, not only to assure verbal subscription of its
tenets, but to further its active implementation.
By the conclusion of Convention 1964, we had
instaUed our full time staflF and amended our Consti
tution so as to make it more effective. We encouraged
each of our
chapters to
adopt an individual chapter
program, which, as it is placed in operation, will align
each of our
operations with the recommendations
of our
Chapter Standards. Our staflF has steadily
improved their knowledge and techniques and, as a
result, we have considerably strengthened some of
our weaker chapters.
Our studies and our work have convinced us of
the importance of rushing operations. It is obvious
that in order to fulfill the purpose of the Psi Upsilon
Program, that we need men of talent, men of promise,
men who have a real sense of "going places." Inas
much as we have a
program which should attract this
type of young man, we must establish rushing pro
grams which will bring them home.
Psi Upsilon has no room for "sitters" or "do nothings."
Our Program calls for "doers" only. We will ferret
out all those who do not strive to do something with
themselves, who do not wish to aid the programs of
their college or of Psi U. We have no room for those
who lower the "will to do" of our members or who
do not wish to carry their full share of responsibility.
It is best to avoid the pledging of these apathetic
characters in the first place.
Thus, an eflBcient rushing program, designed to
meet the circumstances peculiar to each chapter, is
one of our
greatest needs. Some of our units are
eminently successful in avoiding the pitfalls of poorly
planned rushing operations. There is no reason why
all of Psi Upsilon, with the help of our staflF, should
not meet this particular problem with increasing suc
cess. EflFective rushing, then, will be the cardinal
theme for the activities of Psi U for next year.
We will have a
specifically designed campaign,
among others, for those chapters which rush fresh
men at the beginning of the fall semester. This plan
will include the cultivation of secondary school men
in the spring of their senior year. Alumni and actives
should check the qualifications of the incoming fresh
men at the residence level in order to select outstand
ing candidates. We will aid in the organization of
gatherings in the home towns of promising young
men. We will endeavor to perfect a
system that weeds
out those candidates with poor academic records.
Suggestions and modifications by the individual chap
ters to our
general plan, necessitated by specific cir
cumstances on the local level are not only welcome,
but vitally necessary.
The above general outline of one
phase of rushing
techniques is just a small beginning in an over-all
plan to improve our
operations in order to make Psi
Upsilon the finest fratemity, wherein its members are
inspired to live up to their greatest potential and
thereby secure the maximum benefit from their col
lege education. I believe that I can indicate to our
constituency that, as these rushing programs are de
veloped and put into eflFect, we will be even more
proud of the accomplishments of our active brothers.
It is my earnest hope that each Alumnus, as he is
asked to cooperate in the furtherance of the aforemen
tioned plans, will do his part.
Robert W. Paesons, Xi '22
President, Executive Council

Amos Alonzo Stagg, Beta '88
Amos Alonzo Stagg, Beta '88, was
bom in West Orange, New Jersey, on
August 16, 1862, a
year before the
Gettysburg Address and seven years
before Rutgers and Princeton began
American collegiate football.
His origins and early life were con
siderably less than modest. He was
the fifth of eight children born to a
shoemaker and general laborer. His
early character was
shaped by pover
ty, principle and hard work.
This descendant of Colonial Ameri
can stock, removed from the Revolu
tion by less than a
century, was
grad
uated from Orange High School after
three years. He attended Phillips-Exe
ter Academy for a
year, supporting
himself by waiting on tables and sur
vived a bitter winter in a
dingy garret
room. His diet consisted basically of
soda crackers. He could not afford un
derwear, much less heat.
He entered Yale in 1884, a school
that he always admired. Again he
lived on a starvation diet. This time,
however, he became ill. To support
himself and avoid another occurrence
of malnutrition he took odd jobs
around the campus.
Baseball First
Stagg's athletic reputation at Yale
was based primarily on his baseball
ability. He was
generally conceded to
be the best college pitcher of his era
and captained the Eli in 1888. That
year he set a record by striking out 20
against Princeton. During his stay at
Yale, the Eli never lost a
Big Three
game.
Stagg received many substantial
offers to tum professional, but refused
all, choosing not to associate himseff
with what he considered the looseprincipled professional athletes of his
time. He later explained "There was a
bar in every park and the whole tone
of the game was
smelly."
His early relationship with football
could best be described as a
slight
flirtation; it was a new
game to him.
He had seen his first coUege game in
1883 and tried it out briefly during
the two following years.

". . . Called To Preach"
The late '80's and early '90's were
years of decision for young Stagg. His
great motivation had been a desire to
join the ministry, hence a
year of
study at the Yale Divinity School. But
he felt that his speaking ability was
not adequate for the requirements of
the ministry. He commented quite
frankly about his decision: 'T felt spe
cially called to preach, but I decided
to do it on the football field."
He left the Divinity School to be
come a
faculty member at the Inter
national YMCA Training School in
Springfield, Massachusetts. There he
set the course for his life by agreeing
to coach football in the first year of
Springfield CoUege.
The relatively unbuilt University of
Chicago offered Stagg $2,500 a
year
to organize an athletic program in the
summer of 1892.
When he arrived to accept the offer
of Doctor William Harper, Jim Corbett had just won the heavyweight
championship by beating John L. Sul
livan and the American League was
still eight years away from its birth.
A Spectacular Success
His 41 years at Chicago were
spec
tacularly successful. His football
teams had a
composite record of
229-108-27 and outscored their oppo
nents 5827-2724. His teams won
seven Westem Conference (Big Ten)
championships.
Stagg's success was not limited to
the gridiron. His indoor track teams
were three times Westem Conference
champions and his baseball teams
won five Big Ten championships.
In 1910, Stagg took his Chicago
baseball team on an exhibition tour of
Japan. This and several retum trips
helped to establish baseball as a fa
vorite pastime of Japan.
Stagg "retired" from the University
of Chicago and became head football
coach at the College of the Pacific at
the age of 71. He held this position
for 15 years before moving on to as
sist his son, Amos Jr., at
Susquehanna.
His football accomplishments were
far from finished. He was named
"Coach of the Year" by the FootbaU
Writers Association in 1943 after his
COP team
compiled a 7-2 record with
wins over the University of California,
UCLA and Saint Mary's. He was 81
at the time and the United States was
at war.
As his son's assistant at
Susquehan
na, he helped to produce an unde
feated team in 1951; it was the first
in the school's history. By this time,
Milton Berle was Mr. Television.
Because of the health of his wife,
SteUa, he was forced to move West
again in 1953 and assumed advisory
coaching duties at Stockton Junior
College. He finally retired completely
from football in 1960 after coaching
for 70 consecutive years.
He is the only man to be named to
the Football Hall of Fame as both a
player and a coach. He appeared on
the cover of Time magazine on Octo
ber 20, 1958, in connection with an
article appropriately entitled "Grow
ing Old Usefully."
Football's Greatest Innovator
During his last season as a
player
at Yale he first displayed the genious
that made him the greatest innovator
in football history. He rolled up a
gymnasium mat and strapped it, thus
creating football's first blocking and
tackling dummy.
He paved the way for wingback
formations by withdrawing the ends
from the fine of scrimmage. He de
veloped this in 1891 while coaching
at the Springfield YMCA School.
The delayed handoff after a fake to
a back sent through the line put new
emphasis on
deception. Stagg first
used this at the University of Chicago
in 1893. Stagg called it his "Turtleback" play.
He first employed the fake placekick in 1898 where the kicker simply
picks up the baU and mns around
end.
Stagg did not invent the forward
pass, but he was the first Midwest
coach to use it extensively. In 1906,
certainly the Dark Ages of the for
ward pass, Stagg installed 64 pass
patterns.
In 1915 he instituted the practice
of numbering his players to assist the
spectators. This was
quickly adopted
by coaches coast to coast.
He invented the man-in-motion
play for his All-America halfback,
Kyle Anderson in 1927. He was cred
ited with the first crude experiments
with the T formation in the late '20's,
an offense that was more
fully de
veloped by Clark Shaughnessy and
George Halas. Stagg was also the first
football mentor to employ an unbal
anced line.

gress and the public clamored for an

Amos Alonzo Stagg was an un
flinchingly loyal Psi U. A Beta
brother of the class of '88, he
encouraged his two sons, Alonzo

nity; both did so while they were

R. Bourke Corcoran, former sec
retary of the Executive Council
and one-time president of the Psi
Upsflon Foundation, vvTrote of
Brother Stagg:
"Although I was never in ath
letics I knew and admired him
greatly. He was my good friend
and brother. He was always in
terested in Psi U but remained
strictly neutral as a coach. He
was proud that more Omega
brothers won the coveted "C"

decades."
"He almost always marched
with the Psi U's in the front rank
four abreast at the Interfraternity
Sing. If my memory serves me
correctly, I marched with him at
least 25 times.
"Often he told me how proud
he was of all the time we gave
Psi U, both locally and nationally,
for he thought good fraternity
work and loyal membership could
inspire and lead the young."

Stagg, a member of that group,
raised the strongest voice in defense

Fact and Fiction
When any man lives as
long and
accomplishes as much as Amos Alon
zo
Stagg, it becomes difficult to sepa
rate the man from the legend. Many
anecdotes have been told about him.
Perhaps a better understanding of
what the "Grand Old Man" meant to
collegiate athletics can be gained
from the combination of fact and po
lite fiction.
Some of the best Stagg stories con
cern his beloved vAte, Stella, with
whom he had a
truly remarkable rela
tionship. He met SteUa Robertson on
the Chicago campus, where she was a
coed in 1893. They were married on
September 10, 1894.
When Stagg and his new wife went
off to Cahfornia with his team in '94,
Chicago papers commented: "Coach
Stagg really loves his football. Did
you ever hear of a
bridegroom taking
22 men
along on his honeymoon?"
Beginning in 1908, Stella sat in the
press box diagramming plays and
scouting for her husband. She attend
ed practice sessions, taking notes and
making charts and stiU found time for
her house and children.
One day at Susquehanna, SteUa
disappeared. That evening a frantic
Stagg greeted her as she returned. "I
decided to scout Dickinson," said
bright-eyed and smiling Stella as she
dropped 40 pages of notes on the
table. "By the way, Alonzo, you can
get a
pass receiver behind their left
halfback. He's slow on
covering."
With the score tied at 27 that Sat
urday, the Susquehanna quarterback
faded to pass. The primary receiver
broke past the left halfback in ques
tion, took the pass in stride and
waltzed home for the winning score.
Mrs. Stagg merely nodded her profes
sional approval.
The Stagg code for the word gen
tleman belongs to the age of the black
broadcloth and the swallow tailed
coat. One of his Chicago teams lost a
heartbreaker to Ohio State on a
pat
ently bad call by an official. Stagg
had unveiled a ffanker play which
was
good for 57 yards and the game
winning touchdown. The official,
being unfamiliar with the play, decid
ed that it must be iUegal and nullified
the score. The game ended in a near
riot. When Stagg was accosted by the
army of angry sportswriters in a
postgame interview, he said: "Yes, I am a
Kttle disturbed about the way things
tumed out. I misplaced my topcoat
and Mrs. Stagg will be furious."
When Amos Alonzo Stagg was bom
the United States was involved in a
Civil War. When he began coaching
at the University of Chicago, Knute
Rockne was a four year old in Norway.
When he died, a Russian was taking a
walk in outer space.
The world which Brother Stagg left
was considerably different from the
one which he entered . . . and consid
erably better for his having been there.

R. BOURKE CORCORAN
Omega '15
1892-1965
Few of our
distinguished brothers have given more
of their time, interest and devotion to Psi Upsilon than
did R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15. With his passing
we suffer an
irreparable loss. From the time of his ini
tiation in the Omega chapter at the University of Chi
cago in 1911 until his death, on
April 3, 1965, he gave
over
fifty years of dedicated service to our
Fraternity.
The same zeal, spirit and dedication permeated all the
Fsi U projects with which he was associated. It was
indeed fitting that the Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc.,
should call on his genius for organization and his un
selfish and sincere concern for his brothers.
Brother Corcoran's retirement from an active busi
ness career enabled the Fratemity to utilize full-time
his many qualifications. He served as General Chair
man of the fund-raising drive for the Psi Upsilon Foun
dation, Inc. and was elected president and a director
of the Foundation in October, 1962.
Bourke Corcoran has given over 50 years of devoted
service to Psi U. Even before his election to Council in
1920, Brother Corcoran had served as a
delegate to two
conventions�1914 and 1918.
The prime mover in the revival of The Diamond in
1920, he was its business manager for three years and
served as its editor and a member of the Executive
Council's Committee on The Diamond until Novem
ber, 1934. The successful implementation of a Life
Subscription Fund to endow this publication as a forum
for recording the living history of the Fraternity was a
major accomplishment during this period. Brother Cor
coran contributed the chapter on the history of The
Diamond, "the first college fraternity magazine," for
the Annals of Psi Upsilon. With his return to the Execu
tive Council in 1959, he once
again became chairman
of the Executive Council's committee for the publica
tion of The Diamond.
Brother Corcoran's service on the Executive Council
has been varied and outstanding. He was secretary from
1930-1933. Brother Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99, in his
address at the Fraternity's centennial in 1933 made the
following evaluation of Bourke Corcoran's contribu
tion to Psi U: "Any man who can revive a
dying busi
ness
every month or two, as a vocation, and, on the
side, runs a
Fraternity's correspondence, dinners, mag
azine and mailing list, to say nothing of visiting half a
dozen or more
Chapters each year (with a few Phi Beta
Kappa keys in one
pocket and the wrath of God in the
other) still has marrow in his bones." Brother Corcoran
was
vice-president of Council in 1937-1940. He returned
to Council in 1959 when he was elected an
Honorary
Life Member.
Brother Corcoran's numerous other contributions to
Psi U includes service as
Fratemity Archivist 19281929; supervising the production of the 906-page Direc
tory of the Fratemity, published in 1931; assisting
Brother Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, in setting up the
program for the installation of the Epsilon Phi Chapter
in 1928; and co-author of the History of the Omega
Chapter with Floyd Stauffer, Omega '37, in 1941. The
renovation of the headquarters and archives of the Fra
temity in 1960 were also carried out under Brother
Corcoran's direction.
Brother Corcoran's business activity until his retire
ment was
equally varied and challenging. After several
years with the General Electric Company he became
an account representative at J. Walter Thompson Com
pany. He then became an oflBcial of the newly formed
National Electrical Manufacturers Association. He re
tired in 1958 after years of service as head of the Chi
cago oflBce of the Picker X-Ray Corporation.
More important than a strict factual accounting of
Bourke Corcoran's accomplishments, are the countless
occasions when he has given invaluable behind the
scenes counsel and aid to many undergraduate and
alumni brothers over the years.
When his remains were laid to rest they were carried
on the shoulders of six members of the Epsilon Omega
chapter at Northwestern University.

The rushing market today is far different from 30
years ago. Back in those days we had a
great rushing

. . . and the independents were still living in trees.

just one phase
of rushing-sinking the shaft into any other fraternity
in which a rushee might be interested. We knew that
our
prospect wanted desperately to join a fraternity
-he had to in order to get in out of the rain! All we
had to do was knock the other fratemities out of the

How very different now! Our major rushing obstacles
are no
longer the other Greek letter houses. You have
two much tougher competitors. The first is the great
big, plush dormitory that offers aU the physical com
forts of the Hilton hotels and looks mighty good to
many a freshman. Alongside such dormitories, the
average chapter house looks pretty grubby. A man
usually has to be wUling to accept some
personal dis
comfort today if he wants to be a

petitor today is the widely-circulated suggestion that

temities may be harmful to the process of education.

coming to college
today with that indoctrination. To sell them your
fraternity, you first must sell them the fraternity system.

contemplated in "the good old days."
But, though the problems have changed completely
in the last decade or so, rushing techniques still
follow very much the same old patterns. We still
concentrate on
rushing against each other, and over
look the real competition.
It is high time that we all realize that it's no
longer
good enough, or even
halfway smart, to down-grade
the other fraternities in rush. If the Betas knock the

the DUs knock the Betas, pretty soon the rushee gets
the idea that perhaps the critics were
right . . . fra
ternities are no damned good.

fratemity system is good. There are
many good fra
ternities on
campus. Then, from there, tell the rushee
why your chapter is better�why is should appeal to
him more. Not that Beta is worse, but that you are
better.
The Television Parable

analogy in the market place.
Let's suppose that in your city there are several differ
ent stores selling several different brands of color TV.
You've heard a lot about color TV, pro and con. You've
seen it at a
neighbor's. You've about decided to buy a
set, even
though you realize they're not perfect. So, you
stop in at the store selling Brand A, and the first thing
the salesman does is to tell you why you don't want
Brand B. Their colors are
muddy, repair bills are
high,
pictures aren't reliable. You go down the street to take
a look at Brand B, and that dealer tells you that Brand
A is out of date, their circuitry is poor, their cabinets
are shoddy, their tuning is too complex.
Your reaction quite Hkely will be that perhaps it
isn't wise to buy a color TV set after all. So you go
back home to your old reliable black-and-white set
. . . and color TV has lost a customer. Those salesmen
misjudged the market. They didn't realize that first

tem has lost a

they have nothing to be defensive about�and nothing
to attack each other on.

strong, posi
tive story to sell. Socially, economically, scholastically
(yes, scholastically too) they make sense. A positive
approach in rushing unll benefit the entire fraternity

merchandising axiom is, "You can't knock the competi
tor without degrading your own
product." Another is,
"Sell Benefits." They both apply equally to
rushing.
All fraternities should work together in this program.
Through their Interfraternity Conferences they should
start attacking the real job. The real job isn't to make
more rules which only complicate rushing and discotu-age rushees. The real job isn't to act as a
poHce
force to make sure that no
fraternity violates the
many and awesome
rushing rules that already exist,
and to mete out punishment for each infraction. The

a
stronger and better part of campus life, and to pro
vide environment that will make good prospects want

It is told that on the grounds of Buckingham Palace
a
lighted red lantern had been placed at a certain spot
every night for more than one hundred years. Each
morning for more than a
century, the lantern was
picked up, cleaned, and refilled, and each night a
guard carefully replaced it in that same location. It
finally occurred to someone to question this procedure

really needed.

to eliminate the red lanterns, and to get on with the

There's another selHng axiom which appUes equally
